name: Headache & migraine
tagline: Most are not dangerous. Some are. Know the signs.

urgent.heading: Go to hospital now if
urgent.primary_message: Most headaches are not dangerous. But certain warning signs can mean a stroke, brain bleed, or meningitis. Don't wait — go.
red_flags: Sudden 'thunderclap' headache — worst headache of your life, comes on in seconds
Headache with fever and stiff neck or rash
Headache with confusion, slurred speech, or weakness on one side
Headache after a head injury, especially with vomiting or drowsiness
New headache that wakes you from sleep, or worsens when bending or lying down
Headache with seizures, vision loss, or loss of consciousness

what_is_it.heading: Headache and migraine in plain terms
what_is_it.lede: Most headaches are tension headaches — caused by tight muscles, stress, dehydration, or poor sleep. Migraine is different — a neurological condition where the brain becomes hypersensitive, often with severe pain, nausea, and sensitivity to light and sound.
paragraphs: Tension headaches feel like a tight band around the head, on both sides, dull and steady. Migraines usually pulse on one side, last 4–72 hours, and force you to lie down in a dark room. Cluster headaches are rarer — intense, brief, around one eye.

Most headaches resolve with rest, fluids, and simple painkillers. Frequent or severe headaches need a doctor — not to find a tumour (these are rare) but to find a better treatment than you currently have. Migraine especially has many effective treatments people don't know about.

items.headline: Very common
items.body: Around 12% of South Africans have migraine. Tension headaches affect almost everyone occasionally.

items.headline: Treatable
items.body: Migraine has effective treatments — both for stopping attacks and preventing them. If yours isn't well controlled, better options exist.

items.headline: Painkiller overuse
items.body: Taking simple painkillers more than 2–3 days a week can actually cause more headaches. Talk to a doctor about this — common and treatable.

items.headline: Mostly not serious
items.body: Brain tumours and serious causes are rare. Red flags above mark when to worry — for everything else, it is almost always benign.

pull_quote.text: A migraine is not 'just a bad headache'. It is a neurological event that can leave a person unable to work, drive, or care for children for hours or days. It deserves real treatment.

signs.heading: Telling them apart
signs.lede: Different headaches respond to different treatments — identifying yours helps you treat it.

items.title: Tension headache
items.description: Tight band around the head, both sides, dull and steady. Mild to moderate. No nausea. Often from stress, poor sleep, dehydration, eye strain, or bad posture.

items.title: Migraine
items.description: Throbbing pain often on one side, moderate to severe. Often with nausea, vomiting, light and sound sensitivity. Lasts 4–72 hours. May follow visual aura (zigzags, blind spot).

items.title: Cluster headache
items.description: Sudden, severe, drilling pain around one eye. Eye watering, nasal congestion on same side. Brief (15 min – 3 hours) but multiple attacks per day for weeks. Needs specialist treatment.

myths.heading: What is true and what is not

items.myth: Migraine is just a bad headache.
items.fact: Migraine is a neurological condition that involves changes in brain electrical activity, blood flow, and inflammation. The headache is one symptom of many. It deserves to be taken seriously.

items.myth: If painkillers don't help, nothing will.
items.fact: Migraine-specific treatments — triptans, gepants, and others — work when ordinary painkillers don't. Preventer medications can cut migraine frequency in half. Ask your doctor.
Brain tumours are rare and usually cause specific patterns — worse in mornings, vomiting, neurological symptoms. Most frequent headaches are migraine, tension, or medication-overuse — not tumour.

items.myth: Real men just push through headaches.
items.fact: Migraine affects people of all genders. Ignoring it doesn't make it less neurological. Treatment exists — using it is sensible, not weak.

items.title: For occasional tension headache
items.description: Paracetamol or ibuprofen as directed. Hydrate. Rest in a quiet, dim room. Address triggers — sleep, screen time, stress, eye strain.

items.title: For migraine — act early
items.description: Take pain relief and rest as soon as you notice the migraine starting. Triptans (sumatriptan) work much better at the first sign than when the pain peaks. Talk to a clinic about prescription options.

items.title: Keep a headache diary
items.description: Date, time, type, severity, what helped, possible triggers. Two months of notes will show patterns. Bring the diary to the doctor — far more useful than describing from memory.

items.title: If you take painkillers most days — see a doctor
items.description: Painkiller-overuse headache is common and reversible. Counterintuitively, the treatment is to stop the painkiller. A doctor can help you do this safely.

items.title: If red flags appear — go to hospital
items.description: Sudden severe headache, headache with fever/stiff neck/rash, headache with confusion or weakness — these need urgent assessment.

get_help.heading: Where to go
get_help.lede: Most headaches can be managed at clinic level. Persistent migraine benefits from neurology referral — available through the public system.
